title: They Burned Their Own Scrolls — And It Might Unlock a Lost Roman Library
summary: In 79 C.E., Mount Vesuvius buried the Roman city of Herculaneum in volcanic ash — the same eruption that famously destroyed Pompeii. But the disaster did something strange: it carbonized more than a thousand papyrus scrolls in a local library, turning them into fragile black lumps. Today, the Villa of the Papyri collection is the only intact library known to survive from antiquity. The problem? The scrolls are too brittle to unroll. Past attempts often reduced them to piles of ash, and Italian authorities eventually banned the practice. Douglas Seiler, a researcher with collaborators including Berkeley experts, wanted to read them without touching them. His idea: some ancient inks contained lead. Lead absorbs X-rays far more strongly than carbonized papyrus — about 25 times more — so a scan could reveal writing hidden inside a rolled scroll. To test it, Seiler recreated the catastrophe. He imported papyrus and reed pens from Egypt and lampblack ink from Japan, then paid high school students to write passages from Star Wars, the Bible, and the 1960s show The Outer Limits. Then he burned the scrolls. Using X-ray tomography (also called X-ray CT, a technique that takes 3D images of an object's interior), the team detected the writing clearly. The results appeared Sept. 16 in PLOS ONE. The team also found that a handheld X-ray fluorescence scanner — relatively cheap — can quickly screen scrolls for lead ink, identifying the best candidates for detailed imaging. So far, only a small number of Herculaneum scrolls have been virtually opened, and none were first tested for lead. A systematic search hasn't happened yet, but one earlier researcher did detect lead in a fragment. "The stakes are the largest in the history of Greek literature," said Leah Packard-Grams, a Berkeley papyrologist who consulted on the project. About 1,800 scrolls and fragments survive in Italy, France, and England. Some may hold works by Philodemus, an Epicurean philosopher who lived a century before the eruption. "These are books directly from the ancient world frozen in time," Seiler said.
why_it_matters: Only a tiny fraction of ancient writing survived to the present day, so a method that reads sealed scrolls without destroying them could restore whole books of Greek and Roman thought that have been considered lost forever — and it shows how scanning and imaging technology keeps reopening doors that earlier generations had to leave shut.

They were burned on purpose by Roman soldiers

background_read: Mount Vesuvius (the volcano on Italy's coast) erupted in 79 C.E. and buried both Pompeii and its smaller neighbour Herculaneum under ash and superheated gas; Herculaneum was sealed so tightly that wood, rope and papyrus survived instead of rotting away.

The Villa of the Papyri, a luxury Roman house at Herculaneum, was rediscovered in the 1700s, and early excavators found hundreds of scrolls there — many of them were destroyed by the clumsy methods used to open them at the time.

Philodemus (an Epicurean philosopher who lived in the first century B.C.E.) is the author most often identified in the scrolls read so far; Epicureanism was a Greek philosophy that taught that a calm, simple life free of fear was the greatest good.

Modern teams have tried to read the scrolls without unrolling them, using particle accelerators and X-ray imaging; an international contest called the Vesuvius Challenge has offered prizes to groups who could recover text from a scanned scroll, and several groups have succeeded.

Papyrology (the study of ancient writing on papyrus, a paper-like material made from reeds in Egypt) is a small field, so a single recovered library would multiply the surviving Greek and Roman texts by a large fraction — which is why researchers describe the stakes as enormous.

perspectives.perspective: Optimistic — scholars of the ancient world
perspectives.description: For historians and papyrologists this is a rare chance to add entire new texts to the record of Greek literature. If even a few of the ~1,800 scrolls contain lost plays, poems or philosophical works, our picture of the ancient Mediterranean changes.

The experiment succeeded on modern scrolls that Seiler made and burned himself, not on the real library. The ancient inks may not contain lead at all, and every scan of a fragile artifact carries risk, so some scholars warn against promising breakthroughs before one unopened scroll is actually read.

This follows a familiar pattern: early excavators destroyed what they studied, then non-invasive imaging arrived and made old collections readable again — CT scans of mummies, multi-spectral imaging of erased manuscripts. Technology repeatedly reopens archives that were thought closed.

perspectives.perspective: Forward-looking — the research team and funders
perspectives.description: The cheap handheld scanner is the real strategic piece: it could let libraries screen hundreds of scrolls quickly and prioritize the ones with lead ink. Pair that with automated text recognition and a rare lucky find becomes a systematic pipeline instead of a one-off.
